html:
The Timurid Empire was the Turco-Mongol, Persian-speaking Muslim state founded by Timur in 1370. At its height it ruled Iran, Iraq, Afghanistan and much of Central Asia. After his conquests it became famous less for war than for a cultural flowering at Samarkand and Herat.

Timur's empire began to break up as soon as he died in 1405. His son Shah Rukh held most of it together from Herat until 1447. His grandson Ulugh Beg governed Samarkand and built a famous observatory there.

This was the Timurid Renaissance:

  • Architecture: great tiled mosques, madrasas and tombs, such as the Gur-e Amir and the Registan square in Samarkand.
  • Science: Ulugh Beg's star catalogue, the best since antiquity.
  • Painting: Persian miniature painting at its peak in Herat, with the painter Behzad.
  • Literature: Ali-Shir Nava'i wrote poetry in Chagatai Turkic as well as Persian.

The Timurids kept trade and diplomacy with Ming China; Chinese envoys travelled to Samarkand and Herat.

Politically the dynasty kept shrinking. The Turkmen confederations, the Qara Qoyunlu and then the Aq Qoyunlu, took western Iran. The last great Timurid court was that of Husayn Bayqara at Herat, who died in 1506. The Uzbeks under Muhammad Shaybani then took Samarkand and Herat.

One Timurid prince, Babur, lost Samarkand to the Uzbeks, went south to Kabul, and in 1526 founded the Mughal Empire in India. Timurid art and court culture lived on there.
